text: Epicurus calls time an 'accident of accidents' (symbebekos symbebekoton). What does this phrase imply about time's ontological status?
choices: Time is an incorporeal that subsists alongside bodies as a genuine, objective cosmic interval
Time is a second-order property of events (motions, rests, changes), which are themselves accidents of bodies, so it cannot exist without events
Time is an absolute container that flows uniformly whether or not any events occur
Time is the number of motion with respect to before and after, requiring a soul to count it
explanation: Ordinary accidents belong directly to bodies, but for Epicurus time is an accident of the events bodies undergo — one level further removed — making it doubly derivative and inseparable from change. The subsisting-incorporeal view (choice 0) is the rival Stoic position; the absolute self-flowing container (choice 2) is Newton's view, which the relational Epicurean account explicitly opposes; and choice 3 is Aristotle's definition of time.
